title: The Real Citation and the Fluent Fake

zones.label: Fluent Reference
zones.summary: A model-written reference card looks complete and correct, with a gray tick that nobody has earned. A glance cannot tell a real paper from an invented one.
facts: A fabricated citation has plausible authors, a plausible title, a real-sounding venue and year, and often a correctly formatted DOI, for a paper that does not exist or says something different (Chapter 2).
It arises because a citation has a highly regular structure, so a model can generate a well-formed instance without any lookup (Chapter 2).
Fabricated citations are dangerous precisely because they are well formed: they pass a glance (Chapter 2).
The model has no separate channel for what it is sure of, so a completion cannot be trusted by its tone (Chapter 2).

zones.label: Asking the Model Again
zones.summary: Asking the same model whether its citations are real feels like a check. The answer comes from the same mechanism that wrote the citations, so it carries almost no information.
facts: The model will answer 'are these citations real?' fluently, and that answer is generated by the same mechanism that produced the citations (Chapter 2).
Use the model to format a reference list, not to certify it. Certify with a database lookup you ran yourself (Chapter 2).
The same agent in the same session shares the original error and the context that produced it, so its confirmation carries almost no information (Chapter 17).
An independent check has different failure causes from the thing being checked. Running the same process twice checks nothing (Chapter 17).

zones.label: Same Card, Checked
zones.summary: The reference is identical to the one on the left. What changed is that someone left the model, ran the lookups, opened the paper, and earned the green stamp.
facts: Checking requires leaving the model: resolve the DOI, search the exact title in a bibliographic database, compare authors, venue, and year, and open the paper (Chapter 2).
A short script can read a BibTeX file, resolve every DOI, and flag entries with no DOI or a mismatch, and an agent can write it (Chapter 11).
The same discipline applies when the model is correct. It is cheap to do once and expensive to skip once (Chapter 2).
A verified citation means the paper exists, the details match, and the paper supports the claim (Chapter 2).

zones.label: Does It Exist
zones.summary: First check: does the DOI resolve, and does the exact title appear in a database? A reference that fails here has no paper behind it.
facts: DOI lookup retrieves a paper's metadata from its identifier: doi.org redirects to the publisher's page, and the Crossref registry returns the record as data (Chapter 11).
A well-formed DOI and a real venue do not establish that a paper exists (Chapter 2).
A DOI that resolves to a different paper does not make a record real. In Chapter 2's exercise, one DOI led to an unrelated antenna paper (Chapter 2).
If the exact title is not found, or the DOI resolves to a different paper, the verdict is fabricated (Chapter 2).

zones.label: Do Details Match
zones.summary: Second check: do the authors, venue, and year match the database record? A real paper with wrong details must be corrected before it is cited.
facts: Citation verification confirms that each entry exists and that its authors, venue, year, and title match the database (Chapter 11).
In Chapter 2's exercise, one record gave 2017 and a journal where the database listed 2016 and a different venue. The paper was real and needed correcting before use.
A wrong year or volume does not mean a paper is fabricated. It means the details need fixing (Chapter 2).
BibTeX is plain text and is where fabricated references enter a manuscript, since a model can write a perfectly formatted entry for a paper that does not exist (Chapter 11).

zones.label: Does It Support the Claim
zones.summary: Third check: open the paper and find the sentence it is cited for. This is the one step a script cannot do for you.
facts: The one step that cannot be automated is confirming that the paper supports the sentence it is cited for (Chapter 11).
A primary source check goes to the original: the paper itself and not a summary of it. It takes minutes when the agent supplied the location of every claim (Chapter 17).
A model-written summary may be built from the abstract and the model's expectations, so find the sentence in the paper before you cite a claim (Chapter 11).
Ask the agent for a location with every claim, such as the section and table, so the check takes seconds (Chapter 11).

zones.label: Fabricated
zones.summary: No such paper exists. The venue and volume may be real, which is exactly why the citation looks right.
facts: Citations fail in four ways: fabricated, wrong details, unsupported claim, or verified. Fabricated means no such paper exists (Chapter 2).
In Chapter 2's invented example, the exact title was absent from two databases and the authors had no joint work, yet the venue and volume were real.
Well-formed structure is not evidence of existence (Chapter 2).
The useful move is to discard the reference, ask the model for search terms instead, and run those terms in the database (Chapter 2).

zones.label: Wrong Details
zones.summary: The paper exists, but the year, venue, volume, pages, or an author is wrong. Correct the record before it goes into a manuscript.
facts: Wrong details: the paper exists, but year, venue, volume, pages, or an author is wrong (Chapter 2).
In Chapter 2's exercise, one record named the wrong second author and issue number, though the paper existed and supported the claim.
Compare the entry with what the database shows, not with what the model remembers (Chapter 2).
The verdict order is fabricated first, then wrong details, then unsupported claim, then verified (Chapter 2).

zones.label: Unsupported Claim
zones.summary: The paper exists and the details are right, but it does not say what the model claimed. Only reading the paper catches this.
facts: Unsupported claim: the paper exists and the details are right, but it does not say what the model claimed (Chapter 2).
In Chapter 2's invented example, a paper reported 8.2 ENOB and did not discuss 1 MS/s, while the model claimed 10-bit ENOB at that rate.
A summary that sounds right can state a result the paper does not contain (Chapter 11).
If the paper exists, the claim is not automatically supported. Check the sentence it is cited for (Chapter 2).

quiz.question: Which region shows a reference whose authors, venue, year, and DOI all look right, but where nobody has yet looked anything up?
quiz.explanation: A model-written reference is well formed whether or not the paper exists, so it passes a glance. Only a lookup can tell.

quiz.question: A student pastes a bibliography back into the chat and asks if the citations are real. The reply is a confident yes. Which region explains why that reply proves little?
quiz.explanation: The answer is generated by the same mechanism that produced the citations. Certify with a lookup you ran yourself.

quiz.question: Which region shows the identical reference after someone left the model, ran the lookups, and wrote down the result?
quiz.explanation: Verification means resolving the DOI, comparing the record, and opening the paper, none of which the model can do for itself.

quiz.question: A search of the exact title in two databases returns nothing, and the DOI leads to a paper on a different subject. Which check just failed?
quiz.explanation: If the title is absent or the DOI resolves to a different paper, there is no paper behind the reference.

quiz.question: The title matches a real paper, but the database lists a different year and conference. Which check caught the problem?
quiz.explanation: Authors, venue, and year are compared with the database record. The paper is real, but the entry needs correcting.

quiz.question: The paper is real and the entry is correct, yet the sentence it was cited for appears nowhere in it. Which check is the one a script cannot do for you?
quiz.explanation: Scripts can resolve DOIs and compare fields. Only reading the paper shows whether it says what the citation claims.

quiz.question: The journal name and volume are real, but no paper with this title or these authors can be found anywhere. Which failure card matches?
quiz.explanation: Real venue details are what make an invented citation look right. The paper itself does not exist.

quiz.question: A paper exists and supports the claim, but one author name and the issue number are off. Which failure card is this?
quiz.explanation: The paper is real and relevant. Fix the record from the database before citing.

quiz.question: A model correctly cites a real paper and says it reports 10-bit ENOB at 1 MS/s, but the paper reports about 8 bits and never mentions that rate. Which failure card is this?
quiz.explanation: Existence and correct details are not enough. The paper has to say what the citation says it says.

quiz.question: Which region teaches that the same system should not be asked to confirm its own output, and that changing the method, model, session, or person is what makes a check count?
quiz.explanation: An independent check has different failure causes from the thing checked. The same agent shares the original error.
